q: Which primary amine cannot be prepared in good yield by the Gabriel synthesis (potassium phthalimide, then an alkyl halide, then hydrazine)?
h: The key C–N bond forms when the phthalimide anion displaces a halide. What substrate does that step need?
w: The Gabriel synthesis forms the C–N bond by SN2 attack of the phthalimide anion on an alkyl halide, so it works for methyl, primary and some unhindered secondary halides. 1-Methylcyclohexan-1-amine would require 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane, a tertiary halide that cannot undergo SN2; the basic phthalimide anion instead causes E2 elimination to an alkene.
x: Benzylamine comes from benzyl bromide, an excellent S<sub>N</sub>2 substrate.
Butan-1-amine comes from 1-bromobutane, an unhindered primary halide.
2-Phenylethan-1-amine comes from (2-bromoethyl)benzene, a primary halide that reacts well by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: What is the final organic product of the sequence shown?
h: The phthalimide N is alkylated once; hydrazine then releases the nitrogen with its new alkyl group.
w: KOH removes the acidic N–H of phthalimide (pKa about 8.3). The anion alkylates 1-bromo-3-methylbutane by SN2 to give an N-alkylphthalimide, which cannot be alkylated again because its N has no H and its lone pair is delocalized into two carbonyls. Hydrazine cleaves the imide, releasing 3-methylbutan-1-amine (and phthalhydrazide).
x: A dialkylamine forms in direct alkylation of an amine; the imide nitrogen can be alkylated only once, which is the point of the Gabriel method.
This N-alkylphthalimide is the intermediate before step 3; hydrazine cleaves it to the free amine.
Hydroxide is used only to deprotonate phthalimide; the alkyl halide reacts with the phthalimide anion, so no alcohol forms.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is treated with NaN3 in DMSO, and the product is reduced with LiAlH4 and worked up with water. What is the final product?
h: Decide the mechanism (and stereochemical result) of the azide step. Does the reduction step touch the stereocenter?
w: Azide is a strong nucleophile and DMSO is polar aprotic, so the secondary bromide reacts by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-2-azidobutane (the N3 group takes priority 1, as Br did, so inversion changes R to S). LiAlH4 reduces R–N3 to R–NH2 with loss of N2; no bond to the stereocenter is broken, so the product is (S)-butan-2-amine.
x: Retention would require two inversions or a front-side attack; S<sub>N</sub>2 by azide inverts the stereocenter once.
2-Azidobutane is the intermediate; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the azide to the amine.
Racemization requires a planar carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1); a strong nucleophile in DMSO reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 with clean inversion.

q: Treating ammonia with one equivalent of bromoethane gives a mixture of ethylamine, diethylamine, triethylamine and tetraethylammonium bromide. Why?
c: Each alkylation product is at least as nucleophilic as the amine it came from, so it competes for the bromoethane
Ammonia is too weak a nucleophile to react with bromoethane, so only the amine products react with it
Bromoethane reacts by S<sub>N</sub>1, and the ethyl carbocation is captured by every amine present at equal rates, giving all four
Ethylamine is a weaker base than ammonia, so its salt is deprotonated faster and it is alkylated again
h: Compare the nucleophilicity of NH<sub>3</sub> with that of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.
w: Alkyl groups donate electron density, so ethylamine is a better nucleophile than ammonia, and diethylamine is comparable or better still. As soon as some ethylamine forms, it competes with NH3 for bromoethane, and the process continues to the quaternary salt. That is why each product competes for the alkyl halide, and why indirect routes (Gabriel, azide reduction, reductive amination) are used to make primary amines cleanly.
x: Ammonia does react with bromoethane by S<sub>N</sub>2; it is simply out-competed by the more nucleophilic products.
A primary halide does not ionize to a primary carbocation; the alkylations are S<sub>N</sub>2 reactions.
Ethylamine is a slightly stronger base than ammonia, and over-alkylation results from its greater nucleophilicity, not faster deprotonation.

q: Which carbonyl compound and amine give the target compound shown by reductive amination with NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN (pH about 6)?
h: Reductive amination joins the amine N to the former carbonyl carbon, which ends up as a CH that came from C=O.
w: Disconnect the C–N bond to the benzylic CH2: that carbon was the C=O of an aldehyde, and the N came from a secondary amine. Benzaldehyde and piperidine condense to an iminium ion, which NaBH3CN reduces to N-benzylpiperidine.
x: An alcohol has no C=O, so it cannot condense with the amine to form an iminium ion.
Pyridine is aromatic with no N–H; it cannot form an iminium ion and would not give a saturated piperidine ring.
A carboxylic acid simply forms an ammonium carboxylate salt with the amine, and NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN does not reduce acids or amides.

q: In the reductive amination shown, why is NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN used instead of NaBH<sub>4</sub>?
c: Near pH 6, NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN reduces iminium ions far faster than ketones, so the ketone survives to form the imine
NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN is a stronger hydride donor than NaBH<sub>4</sub>, so it can reduce the C=N bond, which NaBH<sub>4</sub> cannot touch at all
NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN supplies the nitrogen atom of the product through its cyanide ligand, which is reduced to an amine
NaBH<sub>4</sub> would reduce the N–H bond of methylamine to give H<sub>2</sub> gas, so no amine product could form
h: The electron-withdrawing CN makes this borohydride milder. Which electrophile in the flask is the most reactive?
w: The cyano group withdraws electron density from boron, making NaBH3CN a weaker, more selective hydride donor that is stable at mildly acidic pH. Under those conditions the iminium ion (C=N+) formed from cyclohexanone and methylamine is far more electrophilic than the neutral ketone, so the iminium ion is reduced selectively to N-methylcyclohexanamine. NaBH4 would reduce much of the ketone to cyclohexanol before the imine formed.
x: NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN is the weaker hydride donor; its selectivity, not its strength, is the point.
The nitrogen in the product comes from methylamine; cyanide stays on boron.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce N–H bonds of amines; the problem with NaBH<sub>4</sub> is that it reduces the ketone too.

q: Which sequence converts benzyl bromide into 2-phenylethan-1-amine (PhCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>)?
h: Count carbons: the product has one more carbon between the ring and N than the starting material.
w: The target has two carbons between the ring and nitrogen, but benzyl bromide supplies only one. Cyanide adds the extra carbon by SN2 (PhCH2CN), and LiAlH4 reduces the nitrile C≡N to CH2NH2, giving PhCH2CH2NH2.
x: The azide route adds nitrogen but no carbon; it gives benzylamine (PhCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>).
Ammonia gives benzylamine, and CH<sub>3</sub>I then methylates the nitrogen instead of adding a carbon to the chain.
Acid hydrolysis converts the nitrile into phenylacetic acid, not an amine.

q: What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> treats amides differently from esters: the C–N bond survives.
w: LiAlH4 reduces an amide all the way to an amine: hydride adds to C=O, the oxygen leaves as an aluminate to give an iminium ion, and a second hydride reduces it. The C=O becomes CH2 and the N keeps its substituents, so N-methylbenzamide gives N-methyl-1-phenylmethanamine (PhCH2NHCH3).
x: Losing the N-methyl group would require breaking an N–C(alkyl) bond, which LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not do.
Esters are reduced to alcohols because the alkoxy group leaves; in an amide the nitrogen is a much poorer leaving group than the oxygen (expelled as an aluminate), so the C–N bond is kept.
An imine or iminium ion is only an intermediate; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces it on to the amine before workup.

q: Which sequence gives 3-bromoaniline from benzene as the major product?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Fe, HCl; then NaOH
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Fe, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Fe, HCl; then NaOH
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; then H<sub>2</sub>O
h: The two groups are meta. Which of NO<sub>2</sub>, NH<sub>2</sub> and Br is a meta director? Then choose a reducing agent that turns ArNO<sub>2</sub> into ArNH<sub>2</sub>.
w: Only the nitro group directs meta, so it must be on the ring when bromine is introduced: nitration, then Br2/FeBr3 gives 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene. A dissolving-metal reduction (Fe or Sn with HCl, then base to free the amine) converts NO2 into NH2 and leaves the aryl C–Br intact: nitrate, brominate, then Fe/HCl.
x: Reducing first gives aniline, a strong o,p-director that is brominated at 2, 4 and 6, not at the meta position.
Bromine is an o,p-director, so nitrating bromobenzene gives mainly 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene and the para amine after reduction.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce aryl nitro groups cleanly to anilines (it gives azo compounds); Fe, Sn or SnCl<sub>2</sub> with acid, or catalytic hydrogenation, is used.

q: Which sequence converts aniline into 4-bromoaniline as the major product?
c: 1. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O, pyridine  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H  3. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. HCl (to form the anilinium ion)  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. NaOH
1. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O, pyridine  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H  3. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; then H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Free NH<sub>2</sub> is so activating that bromination does not stop after one Br. How can its activating power be turned down temporarily?
w: Aniline reacts with bromine at every open ortho and para position, giving 2,4,6-tribromoaniline even with limited Br2. Acetylating the nitrogen makes the less-activating acetamido group (the N lone pair is shared with C=O), and its bulk favors the para position, so monobromination occurs para. Base hydrolysis then removes the acetyl group: acetylate, brominate, hydrolyze.
x: Unprotected aniline is so activated that bromination continues to 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.
The anilinium ion (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) is a strongly deactivating meta director, so it cannot deliver bromine to the para position.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the amide C=O to CH<sub>2</sub>, giving 4-bromo-N-ethylaniline instead of removing the acetyl group.

q: Treating 4-aminophenol with one equivalent of acetic anhydride gives which compound as the main product?
h: Two nucleophiles compete for one acylating agent. Which is more nucleophilic, a neutral aryl NH<sub>2</sub> or a neutral phenol OH?
w: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so the neutral NH2 lone pair is more available and the amine is the better nucleophile. With one equivalent of anhydride, N-acetylation wins and gives N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide (acetaminophen); the amide formed is also no longer nucleophilic, so the reaction stops there.
x: O-Acylation needs a phenoxide or a large excess of acylating agent; the neutral amine reacts faster.
Acetylating both groups would need two equivalents of anhydride.
Ring acylation is a Friedel–Crafts reaction requiring an acyl chloride and AlCl<sub>3</sub>; acetic anhydride alone acylates the heteroatom.

q: When an amide is made from an acid chloride and an amine, two equivalents of the amine (or one equivalent plus pyridine) are used. Why?
c: The HCl formed would protonate the amine to a non-nucleophilic ammonium salt, so a second base takes it up
The first equivalent of amine adds to the C=O and the second displaces chloride from the intermediate
Two amine molecules are incorporated into each amide product, one on each side of the C=O
The excess amine reduces the acid chloride to an aldehyde, which then reacts with more amine
h: Write the by-product of the substitution and ask what it does to the remaining amine.
w: RCOCl + R′NH2 → RCONHR′ + HCl. The HCl immediately protonates any free amine, and an ammonium ion has no lone pair, so it cannot attack the acid chloride. A second equivalent of the amine, or a cheaper base such as pyridine or Et3N, neutralizes the HCl so all of the valuable amine can react.
x: A single amine molecule both adds to the C=O and, after chloride leaves, loses H<sup>+</sup>; the second equivalent only takes up HCl.
Each amide contains one nitrogen from one amine molecule.
Amines are not reducing agents for acid chlorides; this is a nucleophilic acyl substitution.

q: What is the major alkene formed in the Hofmann elimination sequence shown?
h: A trimethylammonium leaving group removed by E2 behaves differently from a halide: think about which β-hydrogen is removed.
w: Excess CH3I converts the NH2 into –N(CH3)3+ I−; Ag2O/H2O exchanges iodide for hydroxide; heating causes E2 elimination of trimethylamine. Hofmann elimination gives the least substituted alkene: the β-hydrogens on the CH3 group (C1) are removed rather than the single hindered H on C3, so the product is 3-methylbut-1-ene.
x: 2-Methylbut-2-ene is the Zaitsev (more substituted) alkene; the bulky ammonium leaving group steers elimination away from it.
2-Methylbut-1-ene would need a double bond at a carbon that was never bonded to nitrogen.
This 3° amine is the product of incomplete methylation; excess CH<sub>3</sub>I takes N on to the quaternary salt, and heat then eliminates it.

q: N-Methylpiperidine is put through one cycle of Hofmann elimination as shown. What is the organic product?
h: In a ring, losing the ammonium leaving group breaks a ring C–N bond, and the nitrogen stays attached to the other end of the chain.
w: Methylation gives N,N-dimethylpiperidinium ion. On heating with hydroxide, a β-H on a ring carbon is removed and the C–N bond to the adjacent α carbon breaks. Because N is still attached to the carbon on its other side, the ring opens to an acyclic alkenyl amine: N,N-dimethylpent-4-en-1-amine, CH2=CHCH2CH2CH2N(CH3)2. Nitrogen is removed completely only after a second cycle of methylation and elimination.
x: Penta-1,4-diene forms only after a second cycle (CH<sub>3</sub>I, Ag<sub>2</sub>O, heat) on the ring-opened amine.
Hydroxide acts as a base, not a nucleophile, in Hofmann elimination; an alcohol is not formed.
The quaternary hydroxide does eliminate on heating; stopping at the ammonium ion ignores step 3.

q: Heating the ammonium hydroxide shown gives mainly but-1-ene rather than but-2-ene. What is the best explanation?
c: The bulky –N(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group hinders removal of an internal β-H, and the carbanion-like E2 transition state favors the CH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens
Hydroxide is a bulky base, so it can reach only the hydrogens on the terminal CH<sub>3</sub> group of the butyl chain
The reaction goes through a carbocation (E1), and the less substituted alkene forms faster from that carbocation by loss of H<sup>+</sup>
But-1-ene is more stable than but-2-ene, so it accumulates as the thermodynamic product of the elimination on heating
h: The base here is small. What is unusual about this substrate compared with 2-bromobutane?
w: The base (OH−) is small, so the selectivity comes from the leaving group. The large, positively charged –N(CH3)3+ group is a poor leaving group, so C–H breaking runs ahead of C–N breaking (a carbanion-like E2 transition state that favors the more acidic primary hydrogens), and its size makes the anti-periplanar conformations for removing an internal C3 hydrogen crowded. Both effects favor removal of a CH3 hydrogen, giving but-1-ene (Hofmann product).
x: Hydroxide is a small base; the steric bulk that matters belongs to the trimethylammonium leaving group.
Hofmann elimination is an E2 reaction; a 2° carbocation would not form, and E1 would favor the more substituted alkene anyway.
But-2-ene, being more substituted, is the more stable alkene; Hofmann elimination gives the less stable product under kinetic control.
